extracted.intended_audience: industrialists, employers, and philanthropists (wealthy donors and company managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical standards and tactics for managing employer–worker relations in heavy industry and for distributing large private wealth via philanthropy and endowed institutions. Covers wage systems, worker benefits, dispute-resolution tactics, and principles for charitable gifts and foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor agreements; discourage breach of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat signed agreements as binding; do not reward or re-negotiate with men who break an agreement, since breaking an agreement undermines future agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie refused to yield when men threatened to break an existing agreement; he emphasized that the worst day for labor is that in which it dishonors itself by breaking its agreement. Enforce agreements firmly to discourage future breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal courtesy and sincere interest in workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet and receive workers with genuine courtesy; show personal interest and appreciation in order to reduce quarrels and build loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie states he always enjoyed meeting his men and that recognition, sincere interest, and kind treatment are the best preventives of quarrels. Practical acts of courtesy and knowing workers by name pay large dividends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sliding wage scale tied to product prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a sliding scale for wages based on the market price of the product so capital and labor share prosperity and adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a scale should include a minimum (living wages), and—preferably—no fixed short term end date; instead make it subject to six months' or a year's notice on either side. Example: a three-year sliding scale was adopted (1889) and ran successfully for decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require individual worker signatures as well as union officer signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow union officers to sign to avoid grievance, but require every workman to sign individually to ensure the agreement binds each man and to reduce union leverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie allowed officers to sign yet required each workman to sign; as a result union officers often did not sign, the union was deserted (no dues), and the union lost its pull—this tactic removed a grievance pretext without direct confrontation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase pay frequency (biweekly pay) to reduce indebtedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay workers every two weeks instead of monthly to help them avoid storekeeper debt and effectively improve real household finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paying fortnightly may cost extra clerical work but can be as valuable to prudent workers as a 10% wage increase; Carnegie implemented this change after workers raised the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate worker coöperative retail (company-supported co-op stores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Help set up cooperative stores for employees by providing support such as rent while workers take responsibility for stock and management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's company paid rent for a coöperative society while men supplied and ran the stock; this taught workers about the difficulties of business and benefited them materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide essential goods at net cost and deliver to homes
rubrics_metrics.description: Company should sell necessities (example: coal) to employees at the company's net cost and arrange home delivery to reduce living expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This measure materially improved workers' living standards (coal sold at about half local dealer prices) and removed a common source of grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer company savings/trust plan with interest and housing loans
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept and safeguard employees' savings (up to a set limit), pay a market interest rate, keep funds separate from business, and lend for home-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie proposed taking savings up to $2,000 and paying 6% interest; funds were kept in a trust and used to lend to employees for homes—encourages thrift and home ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small non-monetary concessions and appreciation often outweigh wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation, kind treatment, fair dealing, and small practical concessions can be as important as, or more important than, higher wages in preventing labor disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include timely pay, selling coal at cost, cooperative stores, and personal recognition—these low-cost measures produced high returns in loyalty and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use firm but nonviolent assertion of authority in meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assert authority through demeanor and rules of conduct (e.g., insisting on civility) to neutralize bullies and preserve orderly negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes forcing a ringleader to remove his hat in a meeting—symbolic rebukes and setting decorum can remove an instigator's influence without physical conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unwilling to fight labor but prepared to be decisively firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a stance of not seeking violent conflict with labor, yet be prepared to hold firm and outlast tactics like 'sitting down' strikes by setting uncompromising conditions for resumption of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie said 'I will not fight, but I can beat any committee that was ever made at sitting down' and required a two‑thirds worker vote for restarting the works—combine moral refusal to fight with clear, enforceable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hospitality and distraction to defuse tensions and build rapport
rubrics_metrics.description: Host committees informally, entertain them (e.g., show them the city, share a meal), and postpone contentious topics until rapport is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie took a committee to Fifth Avenue and to lunch and deliberately avoided discussing the dispute, which helped them later vote to start the mills—building relationship can change votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstate peaceful workers and drop punitive litigation after disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: After strikes and disturbances, promptly dismiss suits against nonviolent workers and rehire those not guilty of violence to restore harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Homestead disturbances, suits were dismissed and old men who had not been violent were taken back—this helps reconciliation and rebuilds loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin distribution of surplus wealth with workers (relief funds/pensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use surplus wealth first to benefit workmen directly—establish relief funds for accidents, small pensions for old age, and other employee-focused endowments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's first distribution on retiring included 4 million in bonds for an 'Andrew Carnegie Relief Fund' and 1 million for libraries/halls for workmen; the relief fund provided pensions and accident relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropic gifts can be made anonymously or through intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Donors may give through others or anonymously to ensure beneficiaries do not attach the donor's name or to counter claims of self-promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes instances where he had given money through others without publicity (example of McLuckie) and cautions that stories can distort motives—anonymous giving is a valid strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund durable public institutions (libraries, museums, schools) as a form of philanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Endow and build public libraries, museums, technical schools, picture galleries, and other institutions that educate and uplift communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie funded many branch libraries and a group of buildings in Pittsburgh (museum, picture gallery, technical schools, Margaret Morrison School), investing in institutions that return lasting public value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create endowed research institutions with a broad cooperative mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Found and endow institutions dedicated to encouraging research, discovery, and the application of knowledge, with a charter to cooperate widely across governments and educational bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's charter for the Carnegie Institution: 'To encourage in the broadest and most liberal manner investigations, research and discovery, and the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind' and explicitly to cooperate with governments, universities, colleges, technical schools, learned societies, and individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer returning benefits to communities where wealth was created
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider prioritizing philanthropic investments in the cities or regions that contributed to the donor's fortune as a matter of justice and gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie emphasizes returning to Pittsburgh (where he made his fortune) through major gifts, noting the city's contributions and the partial restitution via public institutions.
